events.title: The king holds the hill and gives it to none
events.body: The king tells the gathered claimants that no line among them is better than another and that Catrìona Mhòr's line cannot be handed to a stranger's open palm; he will hold the hill himself, as before Gormshuil first took it up in his name.

events.title: The first marriage reckoned openly for a share
events.body: A young man of a minor line is married to a woman three lines removed from the king, and his father says openly at the betrothal fire that the match is made to bring five lines instead of three nearer the front of the reckoning, should the king ever name an heir.

events.title: A daughters' claim disputed at a betrothal
events.body: A household holding good grazing but no claim of its own is joined by marriage to one that claims through four generations of daughters, and the hill argues without settling whether a claim run through daughters weighs more or less than one run through sons.

events.title: A betrothal broken over a nearer claim
events.body: A grandmother breaks off her granddaughter's marriage within the month of its making, having found a nearer claim on the groom's own side that she judges would weigh the match's worth downward; the hill takes it as proof that every marriage among the blood is now made for its shares and not for anything else.

events.title: A household of the western slopes loses its grazing
events.body: A household that has held grazing on the western slopes eleven generations is told, without reason given, to remove itself to ground of equal size two valleys over before winter; asked directly why, the king says only that a share given has always been a share that can be taken back.

events.title: Raonaid nic Ailein dies at the river-meadow
events.body: Raonaid nic Ailein, the king's daughter, dies at her own river-meadow in her one thousand three hundred and eightieth year; the king sits with her the better part of a day and a night, as he sat once with Gormshuil and once with Somhairle, and speaks of it to no one after.

events.title: The king takes back Raonaid's grazing
events.body: Within the month of Raonaid nic Ailein's burying the king sends word that the river-meadow grazing is wanted elsewhere and that Niall Òg, her nearest of that line, is to remove his household from it; Niall answers, as he has come to answer every such word, with a laugh.

events.title: The king sends Niall Òg to Dùn dhearg
events.body: The king chooses Niall Òg to carry word east of the vein, bidding the households of Dùn dhearg come in to him at last, judging that a man known for asking nothing on his own account is less likely to be mistaken for the leading edge of a conquest.

events.title: Niall Òg finds Dùn dhearg wanting nothing of the hill
events.body: Niall Òg crosses the vein and finds the double bank of Dùn dhearg larger and better kept than any western telling had prepared him for, its forges and granary proof of a country that has gone far, by its own hands, toward needing nothing from Dùn ìseal.

events.title: Fearghal Donn refuses the king's asking
events.body: Fearghal Donn, holder of Dùn dhearg, hears the king's messenger before the whole household and answers that his people have raised their own bank and buried their own dead without any man's leave, and will not be counted among a kin who marry for shares and wait a thousand years for a hill never given.

events.title: Niall Òg carries the refusal home
events.body: Niall Òg rides back to Dùn ìseal and gives Fearghal Donn's word to the king plainly; the king says he had looked for no other answer, thanks him for the carrying of it, and turns to the next claim waiting for him.

events.title: The spears of the east are kept to hand
events.body: Word reaches Dùn ìseal by traders, not by any messenger sent for the purpose, that the households about Dùn dhearg have begun keeping their own spears closer than ever before, against a quarrel none of them will name; the king does nothing about it that anyone can see.

events.title: A woman of Clann na Ceiste speaks over the child
events.body: An old woman of Clann na Ceiste, come down from the slab to see the new child, tells Gille-Brìde that a boy born short-lived among the long-lived will learn early what his own kin have never needed to learn until late: how much of a life can be made to matter in however much of it is given.

events.title: Ceallach is born in the high valleys
events.body: A son is born to Gille-Brìde of Somhairle's line in the high valleys and is called Ceallach; he is slower to walk and to run than the children before him, the first sign, told back afterward, that the years were coming down faster in him than in his father.

events.title: Fearghal Donn dies at Dùn dhearg
events.body: Fearghal Donn, who had held Dùn dhearg since before Niall Òg was sent to him and sent back with nothing, dies an old man in his own bed at the fort; the households east of the vein bury him as they buried Ailis, without word sent to the hill and none expected back.

events.title: Artair takes up the holding of Dùn dhearg
events.body: Artair, Fearghal Donn's son, takes up the holding of Dùn dhearg with no more ceremony than his father had used, and says at the burying itself that he will hold what his father held and ask nothing further of the hill until the day it asks something of him.

events.title: Gille-Brìde's father dies in his three hundred and eighth year
events.body: Gille-Brìde's father dies at Samhain in his three hundred and eighth year, fewer years than his own father had, dying as most of that line has learned to die: without illness or wound, simply slower each year until one morning he does not rise from his own hearthstone.

events.title: Word runs that the kin will gather below Dùn ìseal
events.body: At the burying, word runs among the fires that the king's kin mean at last to come down out of their scattered holdings and gather in the valley below Dùn ìseal, each line with its own tents and its own fire, to wait together upon the shares left uncounted since Catrìona Mhòr's death.

events.title: The kin come down household by household
events.body: Through the summer the king's kin come down into the valley below Dùn ìseal household by household and line by line, no single word sent to call any of them, until the valley holds more tents and more fires than any one household has ever seen gathered in one place.

events.title: Murchadh Mòr brings his sons and grandsons down
events.body: Murchadh Mòr comes down from the northern plain with a column of sons and grandsons that takes three days to pass any one point on the road, carrying more tent-cloth, it is said, than the valley below Dùn ìseal has ever seen brought to one place at once.

events.title: Eithne's knot-keeper counts every soul on the new ground
events.body: Eithne comes down from the southern outpost with her own household, and her knot-keeper walks at its head with the household's cord wound about his arm, meaning to be seen keeping count of every soul who sets foot on the new ground, and does so from the first day to the last.

events.title: Ìomhar Dearg pitches nearest the vein
events.body: Ìomhar Dearg comes down from the eastern marches nursing a hundred years' grievance over river-grazing he judges his by use if not by the king's word, and pitches his tents nearer the vein than any other line thinks wise, exactly, everyone agrees, like him.

events.title: Sìne nan Snaidhm keeps the cord of the whole valley
events.body: Sìne nan Snaidhm, knot-keeper of the household cord at Dùn ìseal, walks the growing valley of tents checking each new fire against the cord she carries, so that within a season no soul is pitched there, of the king's blood or of any household following it down, whose count she has not kept.

events.title: A steward is set over every line
events.body: By the second summer a steward stands over every line camped below Dùn ìseal, holding no ground and no lordship, only charged to speak for its household at the common fires and see its people fed and housed while the waiting goes on, until the valley looks less like a gathering than a town that never raised walls.

events.title: The host of the east begins to gather at Dùn dhearg
events.body: In the spring the host of the east begins gathering at Dùn dhearg under Artair, who is said to have waited three years, since he first took up his father's holding, for the very stillness of the hill to break; word of the gathering reaches the western fires within the week.

events.title: Gille-Brìde and Ceallach come down to see the valley
events.body: Gille-Brìde walks down out of the high valleys with Ceallach, now grown but already, though neither says it, walking more slowly than a man of his years should, and the two stand at evening looking over more fires than either has ever seen gathered at once.

events.title: Sìne nan Snaidhm names Gille-Brìde the one soul asking nothing
events.body: Sìne nan Snaidhm tells Gille-Brìde that his name is on no cord she carries, since he has asked for no ground and no share from anyone, and that he is, that night, the only soul in the whole valley of whom that can be said.

events.title: The king goes down to meet the east with a handful of household
events.body: Near the end of summer the king comes down from Dùn ìseal with no more than three tents' worth of his own household, going to meet the east himself, while every line camped in the valley says, each at its own fire, that it will follow him within a day or two.

events.title: The king sends Gille-Brìde home to the hills
events.body: Gille-Brìde asks the king plainly whether he too should come down to the ford; the king tells him to go home to his own people instead, since whatever comes of it will want telling afterward by someone who was not in it, and his line has always been better at the telling than the coming.

events.title: The host of Dùn dhearg musters at the ford
events.body: Every household east of the vein sends its spears down to the river below Dùn dhearg in the last days of an Lùnastal, camping the whole night along a mile of the east bank under Artair mac Fhearghail, meaning to hold the crossing before the king's kin can gather against them.

events.title: Artair mac Fhearghail recalls the answer sent to the king
events.body: At the fires the first night, Artair mac Fhearghail repeats to the host the answer his father Fearghal Donn once sent back with the king's messenger, that the households east of the vein would keep their own bank and owed the hill at Dùn ìseal nothing, and says the answer has not changed in eighty years.

events.title: The east finds the king alone at the ford
events.body: At sunrise the host of Dùn dhearg finds a single man sitting on the stone at the head of the ford, his kin nowhere on the far bank; word runs down the fires that the king's own household has quarrelled over the shares of his kingdom and would not follow him east.

events.title: The first rush breaks on the king at the ford
events.body: Two hundred spears go into the ford together at sunrise on the first day and are thrown back with the king alone in the water among them; the host sees the river run red below the crossing before the morning mist has fully lifted.

events.title: The east tries the ford's edges and its throwing spears
events.body: Through the first day the host tries the deep channel above and below the ford to come at the king from the side, and by afternoon empties its fletchers' whole store throwing spears from the bank; neither the crossing nor the throwing turns him from his stone.

events.title: A household of Caol shean loses a man to the first day's ford
events.body: A net-mender's kinsman of Caol shean, twenty years unhurt at every boundary quarrel of the eastern country, goes into the first rush and is not seen to come out of the river; his wife asks after him at every fire down the bank until evening, then asks no more.

events.title: The dead of the host begin to dam the ford
events.body: On the second day the drowned and the slain lie so thick at the shallows below the crossing that the river backs up over the gravel, running warm and red, and the men of Dùn dhearg must climb their own dead to reach water shallow enough to cross.

events.title: The king draws a boy of Dùn dhearg from the river with his own hand
events.body: In the press of the second day the king takes the spear from the hands of a sixteen-year-old of the eastern host as a mother takes a knife from a child, and the boy is carried out alive on the east bank; the telling of that hand is kept by the east long after his name is forgotten.

events.title: Artair mac Fhearghail counsels the host to go in together
events.body: On the second night, with some of the host ready to go home, Artair mac Fhearghail tells the fires that the king is flesh and must have an end, as a cliff has an end before the sea, and counsels every spear of the east to go into the river together on the third day and not draw back.

events.title: The whole strength of the east goes into the river together
events.body: At first light on the third day every spear the east country has enters the ford at once and does not draw back, the host closing on the king from three sides the whole day long while the dead already in the water rise higher than the shallows had ever stood.

events.title: A light is seen on the water around the king
events.body: In the afternoon of the third day men near the middle of the ford see a light low along the river's surface where the king stands, of no colour any of them had a word for, and say afterward only that they saw every colour in it and none, and would say no more.

events.title: The king's kin fail to come to the ford
events.body: Through all three days at the ford below Dùn dhearg, no household of the king's own blood, and no spear of the hills, comes down the western track to stand with him; the host of the east has the river to itself the whole time.
